Questions 6 – 7 were notably more challenging and provided good discrimination at the top end.
Students are generally much better now at carrying out standard statistical calculations but interpreting these, as was required in question 1(e) is still proving a challenge to most.
It was rare to see an error in part (a) but many students did not know a suitable formula for finding the variance and failed to score marks in part (b) or part (d)(ii).
Part (c) proved to be a good discriminator with many failing to see the connection with part (b) but others identifying class B because the variance was larger.

Very few had any problem in finding the correct mean in part (d)(i) but good answers to part (e) were far less common with weaker students failing to give supporting reasons or simply stating that coding makes no difference.
In part (i) many mentioned that the variance would not change because the data was coded which is of course insufficient.
The key here is that variance is unchanged because the “coding” only involves addition.

Part (ii) was more often correct and the examiners did condone the calculation of the new mean, as this was so straightforward, though all that was required was a statement that the total score had increased.

Part (iii) was the most challenging: many simply stated that the variance would increase because the marks were only added to one class but, of course, had they been added to class B then the mean of class B would be closer to the mean of class A and the opposite conclusion would apply.
Part (a) proved surprisingly challenging with many forgetting to include A B ∩ in their shading or shading A B′ ∩ .
notes.display: Part (a) proved surprisingly challenging with many forgetting to include $A \cap B$ in their shading or shading $A \cap B'$.

notes.quote: Part (d) was the most challenging part and only a few realised that a conditional probability was required and even fewer gave a correct ratio.
In part (e) a number successfully gave one correct product of probabilities but it was rare to see all 4 and the correct answer.

The standard probability calculation involving the normal distribution in part (a) was answered quite well though it is disappointing to see some have a correct statement such as P(Z > – 0.4) followed by a probability less than 0.5 The rest of the question got progressively more challenging.

In part (b) many muddled their way through to obtain 180 15 k − = to a z value with |z| > 1.5 and many had a value of 1.96 but the correct sign was less frequently seen so only the stronger students had a correct answer of 150.6 Part (c) provided a good challenge for the best students at the end of this paper.
notes.display: In part (b) many muddled their way through to obtain $\frac{k-180}{15}$ to a z value with |z| > 1.5 and many had a value of 1.96 but the correct sign was less frequently seen so only the stronger students had a correct answer of 150.6 Part (c) provided a good challenge for the best students at the end of this paper.

notes.quote: There were plenty of attempts at standardising with the relevant means and standard deviations but few were able to form a correct equation in w, the usual problem was a missing minus sign which led to an incorrect value of w = 144 A further mark for attempting to use this value was often obtained but only the very best students achieved the correct answer of 0.212 Pearson Education Limited.
